changes.title: The observations become paired
changes.before: You compare mean handling times for two independent groups of 30 teams. A Welch independent-samples t-test is your starting point.
changes.change: You learn that the two lists are actually the same 30 teams, measured before and after a change.

choices.label: Keep the independent-samples analysis unchanged.
choices.feedback: This ignores the matching. The observations in the two lists are related.

choices.label: Analyse within-team differences and revisit the assumptions.
choices.feedback: The pairing changes the sampling design. A paired t-test may fit the mean-difference question after checking the differences.

choices.label: Replace the comparison with correlation only.
choices.feedback: A strong before/after association does not establish a mean improvement.

changes.explanation: Verify the pair identifiers and investigate missing pairs. Examine the distribution and outliers of the team-level differences and independence between teams. A paired t-test addresses whether the mean difference is zero; report the estimated change and interval. Consider a suitable alternative if its assumptions do not fit. Matching alone does not establish that the intervention caused the change.
changes.unchanged: The business question and units can stay the same. The independent-sample assumption and standard-error calculation cannot.
changes.followup: What would you do if six teams had no valid after measurement?

changes.title: A previously unique lookup gains duplicates
changes.before: A left join preserves all request rows. The service lookup has one approved row per service code and the totals reconcile.
changes.change: The next lookup refresh has two different active labels for one service code. The request data is unchanged.

choices.label: Apply DISTINCT to the final output and continue.
choices.feedback: This can hide the symptom or discard legitimate equal records. It does not resolve conflicting labels.

choices.label: Investigate the mapping, obtain an approved resolution and rerun cardinality checks.
choices.feedback: The join type may still fit, but the previously validated relationship no longer holds.

choices.label: Use an inner join instead.
choices.feedback: Both duplicate lookup records still match. Inner versus left does not fix a non-unique key.

changes.explanation: Identify the conflicting key and its downstream rows. Check whether time-effective versions or a compound key were intended; confirm the correct grain with the owner. Do not choose an arbitrary first value. After an authorised resolution, reconcile row counts, distinct request IDs, aggregates and unmatched keys. Add a uniqueness or effective-date check before future joins.
changes.unchanged: Retaining all requests may still require a left join. What changes is the trust in the lookup key and the work needed before using it.
changes.followup: How would the solution differ if both labels were valid in different date periods?

changes.title: A policy changes the demand pattern
changes.before: A forecasting model is evaluated with rolling time windows on five years of monthly demand. It performs better than a seasonal-naive baseline.
changes.change: A new eligibility policy starts next month and could change both the number and type of requests. No post-policy actuals exist yet.

choices.label: Publish the historical forecast as a dependable policy forecast.
choices.feedback: Past accuracy does not establish performance after a structural change.

choices.label: Explain the break, compare justified scenarios and plan monitoring.
choices.feedback: A conditional baseline and explicit assumptions are more defensible than claiming the model has learned a policy that has not occurred.

choices.label: Discard the history and invent a new point estimate.
choices.feedback: Losing useful context and inventing a precise estimate does not solve the uncertainty.

changes.explanation: Clarify the policy mechanism with the owner. Keep a labelled no-change baseline and develop documented scenarios with plausible assumptions; scenarios are not automatically probabilistic intervals. State that the historical model has not been validated under the new policy. Agree a monitoring/retraining plan, collect post-change actuals and compare models when enough relevant evidence exists.
changes.unchanged: The forecasting horizon, decision and error measures may remain useful. Assumptions about stability, training relevance and uncertainty need another review.
changes.followup: Which early indicators would make you revise a scenario before a full month of outcomes is available?

briefings.title: Synthetic service demand
briefings.question: How should the service lead respond to the recent increase in requests?
facts: April received 100 requests and May 110: an increase of 10 requests, or 10%.
The counts use the same service definition and complete monthly extracts.
Two months do not establish a trend, seasonal pattern or cause. Staffing capacity and request complexity have not been measured.

lead.question: Does May demand justify a staffing decision?
lead.finding: May received 110 requests, 10 more than April (+10%).
lead.uncertainty: Two months alone do not establish sustained growth, and we have not assessed request complexity or spare capacity.
lead.action: Review capacity and a longer history before changing staffing; monitor the next monthly extract.

technical.question: Can the month-to-month comparison support a capacity recommendation?
technical.finding: Under the same service definition, monthly counts rose from 100 to 110; (110−100)/100 = 10%.
technical.uncertainty: Extracts are complete, but there are only two time points and no adjustment for working days or case mix. No causal or forecasting claim is supported.
technical.action: Validate comparable exposure periods and analyse a longer series with case mix and capacity before modelling staffing needs.

briefings.title: Synthetic missing completion dates
briefings.question: Can the completion-time dashboard be used in the briefing?
facts: A synthetic extract contains 200 completed requests; 20 lack a completion date (10%).
The reported median of 6 days was calculated from the remaining 180 records.
No investigation has established whether missing dates are related to longer waits.

lead.question: Can we rely on the reported median completion time?
lead.finding: The median is 6 days among 180 records with usable dates; 20 of 200 records were excluded.
lead.uncertainty: The excluded 10% may differ from the rest, so this is not yet a dependable summary of all completed requests.
lead.action: Label the coverage, ask the data owner to investigate missing dates and revisit the briefing after validation.

technical.question: How does missingness affect the completion-time estimate?
technical.finding: Complete-case median = 6 days, n=180; completion dates are missing for 20/200 completed records.
technical.uncertainty: The missingness mechanism is unknown. Complete-case analysis can be biased if missing dates relate to duration; filling them with zero would change the meaning.
technical.action: Profile missingness by source and service, investigate with the owner, and assess a justified sensitivity analysis before finalising the statistic.

briefings.title: My own sanitised findings
briefings.question: Use your own approved findings and reference IDs.
facts: State the population, period, units and denominator for any figures.
Separate observed findings from assumptions, forecasts and recommendations.
Use sanitised summaries; keep original workplace data in approved storage.

audiences.label: Senior decision-maker
audiences.guidance: Lead with the decision and the important finding. Explain uncertainty in plain language and end with a proportionate action.

audiences.label: Technical colleague
audiences.guidance: Include definitions, denominators, method and validation details. State assumptions, limitations and the next analytical check.
